claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi is an example of a single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
Enhanced hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys arise from a deformation-induced local transformation at grain boundaries.
Deformation-induced transformation creates ultrafine amorphous or highly disordered grain-boundary layers.
Deformation promotes short-range chemical ordering in the grain-boundary regions.
The proposed dynamic transformation becomes active at nanocrystalline grain sizes in the inverse Hall–Petch regime.
Amorphous or highly disordered interfacial regions impede dislocation motion.
Short-range chemical ordering stabilizes the transformed interfacial regions.
Local stress concentrations at grain boundaries trigger partial amorphization under high strain.
Severe deformation can produce an ultrananocrystalline layer in CoCrFeMnNi.
Dislocation behavior in high-entropy alloys is modified at dislocation cores and boundaries.
The transformed interfacial regions increase resistance to shear and thereby increase hardness and yield strength.
Nanocrystalline, partially amorphized or ordered samples will have significantly greater hardness and yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline.
TEM should reveal ultrafine boundaries with amorphous, highly disordered, or short-range-ordered structures in the deformed samples.
The relevant nanocrystalline regime is typically below approximately 100 nm.
Suppressing oxidation with an inert environment reduces extrinsic oxidation effects on the comparison.
The proposed mechanism generalizes to single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys but may not apply to multiphase alloys or substantially different chemistries.
Failure to observe both the proposed interfacial transformation or increased short-range order and a statistically significant strength or hardness increase would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels the behavior inverse Hall–Petch-like while attributing increased strength to further grain refinement and stronger barriers. That causal direction describes conventional Hall–Petch strengthening, whereas inverse Hall–Petch behavior denotes decreasing strength with decreasing grain size within the inverse regime.
